chapters.title: A bridge between dies
chapters.text: From above, find the narrow connection zone between neighboring dies. A local silicon bridge concentrates fine routing where a crossing is needed, while the substrate serves the surrounding area. Locate the bridge first, then ask why the whole package floor does not need to become one.

chapters.title: Bridge versus full platform
chapters.text: Highlight the bridge to distinguish it from a broad interposer. Both support heterogeneous integration, but distribute fine routing differently. This model explains a bridge embedded in a substrate; bridge-based products can differ in structure, so the illustration is not a universal vendor structure.

chapters.title: Die edges are the shoreline
chapters.text: Fly along facing die edges. Bridge channels must meet the intended contacts; rotating a die arbitrarily will not make compatible wiring appear. Available die-edge length, contact placement and interface orientation belong in the system floorplan, before the bridge is treated as a finished connection.

chapters.title: Integrate the bridge
chapters.text: Descend toward the substrate. The bridge and surrounding material must create an assembly-compatible surface. Embedding, alignment, die placement and contact formation all have tolerances. This sequence explains assembly relationships, not a particular machine recipe; actual work follows qualified process documentation.

chapters.title: Which routes use the bridge?
chapters.text: In the separated-layer view, trace die-to-die signals separately from power and external connections toward the substrate. They need not all cross the same bridge. Some bridge technologies add vertical structures, so this simplified view must not be used to infer every product’s power-delivery arrangement.

chapters.title: A bridge needs an interface
chapters.text: Glowing paths show geometric connectivity. Communication still requires compatible signaling and protocols at both ends. A bridge is a physical integration approach, not a single communication standard. The UCIe tour separates the question of how roads are built from how participants communicate over them.

chapters.title: Materials heat together
chapters.text: Bridge, substrate and dies are different materials. Temperature changes can create mismatched deformation and concentrate stress near joints. Thermal and mechanical analysis belong together. A small bridge is not automatically free of reliability risk simply because it occupies little area.

chapters.title: Test bridge and system
chapters.text: Check channels for opens and shorts, then verify that the dies exchange correct data under specified conditions. Geometric alignment, electrical continuity and system function are different evidence layers. Diagnose failures by separating joint defects, signal quality and protocol configuration.

chapters.title: Trade-offs of local precision
chapters.text: Local bridges focus precision where it is needed, but constrain floorplanning and substrate integration. Compare more than silicon area: include assembly complexity, supply chain, testing and yield. The right choice serves the complete product, rather than rewarding the most visually appealing structure.

chapters.title: Find the bridge from the need
chapters.text: Return overhead: choose communicating dies, arrange edge interfaces, place bridges, plan power and cooling, then prove cooperation through testing. The visual idea is restraint: reserve precision for critical crossings instead of making every part of the package equally complex.
